title: How Customs Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how customs works, starting with bush meat smuggling through Paris Charles de Gaulle airport, then the origins of US customs in the Tariff Act of July 4, 1789, and its role as a revenue source and the parent of several federal agencies. They cover the 2003 move to US Customs and Border Protection under Homeland Security, its enforcement of about 400 provisions of law, "exodus" cases involving weapons technology, duty-free exemptions (the $400 exemption, tobacco and alcohol allowances, fine art and antiques), the difference between individual travelers and importers, and detection methods such as random number generators, truck-sized X-rays, detector dogs (beagles), and residue-sniffing devices. Smuggling anecdotes (drugs hidden in bodies, pets, frozen sharks, puppies), the Mediterranean fruit fly incident and California agricultural checks, the $10,000 cash limit, antiquities seizures, dog meat and Cuban cigar embargoes follow. The episode closes with a listener email from Sergeant John Walker in Afghanistan.

entities.name: National Institute of Standards and Technology

segments.title: Opening banter and bush meat in Paris
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, then describe bush meat (wild game such as monkey, crocodile, porcupine) found in unrefrigerated luggage of arrivals from Africa at Paris Charles de Gaulle airport, in a 17-day wildlife and customs search.

segments.title: Origins of US customs
segments.summary: Chuck explains the founding-era tariffs under George Washington's first Congress and the Tariff Act of July 4, 1789, signed July 31, 1789. Customs revenue funded government for about a century, with zero debt by 1835, and it remains second only to the IRS in revenue, about $30 billion a year.

segments.title: Agencies spawned by Customs
segments.summary: The Customs Service handled census and veterans affairs functions, helped create the National Institute of Standards and Technology, and gave rise to the Coast Guard. In 2003 it became US Customs and Border Protection under Homeland Security.

segments.title: Enforcement role and exodus cases
segments.summary: Customs controls the flow of goods in and out, seizes contraband, processes people and cargo, and enforces about 400 provisions of law including intellectual property. The hosts describe 'exodus' cases involving weapons and weapons technology, and a recent sting involving batteries for missile launches to Iran.

segments.title: Duties, tariffs and the sombrero example
segments.summary: Explanation of why duties exist: to encourage buying American goods and to collect revenue. The sombrero example shows how duty can make an imported item cost more than a domestic one. NAFTA is mentioned as a complication.

segments.title: Duty-free exemptions
segments.summary: The US allows a $400 duty-free exemption for travelers returning from most places (not Caribbean basin countries, Virgin Islands, Guam, or American Samoa), with specific allowances for cigarettes, cigars and alcohol. Fine art and antiques at least 100 years old are duty free. The exemption applies to the importer, so a traveler buying duty-free abroad and bringing goods into the US pays duty.

segments.title: Screening methods and detection technology
segments.summary: Hosts compare big business importers with individual travelers. Customs inspects randomly, sampling cargo containers and passengers. Some countries use random number generators, or rely on agent intuition. The US uses truck-sized X-rays at the Mexican border, helicopters, jets, and cigarette boats in joint work with the Coast Guard and DEA, and an electro vacuum device that detects residue in the air.

segments.title: Smuggling anecdotes and detector dogs
segments.summary: Stories of smugglers hiding drugs on their bodies, in pet snakes, frozen sharks, puppies and a yellow lab, plus the use of beagles to sniff out agricultural products and bombs. A dog-sniffing check on planes after disembarkation is described. Travelers are often nervous at checkpoints.

segments.title: Agricultural checks and the Mediterranean fruit fly
segments.summary: A single piece of fruit carrying Mediterranean fruit flies in the late 1980s contaminated California crops. California agricultural checkpoints on the Vegas-to-California route are described.

segments.title: Cash limits, antiquities, dog meat and Cuban cigars
segments.summary: The $10,000 cash export limit and suspicion of amounts near it, customs seizures of antiquities including a Chinese sculpture found in an auction catalog and artifacts found in a Bulgarian suitcase, the ban on dog meat, and the Cuban cigar embargo.

segments.title: Listener mail from Sergeant John Walker
segments.summary: A listener email from Sergeant John Walker in Afghanistan says the podcast is popular with his platoon and that he and a friend translate episodes into Farsi for local schoolchildren.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts point listeners to related HowStuffWorks articles on customs and list the listener mail address, then close with an ad.
